subject: Accounting
title: The Break-Even Point
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Break-Even Point usable.

hook.text: A startup sells candles for $20 each. It costs $8 per candle plus $6,000 monthly rent. When does it profit?

buildup.text: The break-even point is where total revenue exactly equals total costs—zero profit, zero loss.

discovery.text: Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ (Price – Variable cost). Here: $6,000 ÷ $12 = 500 candles.

twist.text: Selling 499 candles means a loss. Selling 501 means profit. One sale can flip the outcome.

climax.text: Every business should know its break-even—it's the survival threshold.

punchline.text: Below break-even, you're paying to work.

quiz.question: What is the break-even point?
options: Where total revenue equals total costs

details.summary: The break-even point is the sales volume at which total revenue exactly equals total costs—no profit and no loss. This topic explains how to calculate break-even in units and dollars, graph it, and use it for planning and risk assessment.
details.whyItMatters: Every business needs to know the minimum sales required to avoid losses. Break-even analysis is the simplest yet most powerful tool for understanding the relationship between costs, volume, and profit.
takeaways: Break-even in units equals total fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit
Break-even in dollars equals total fixed costs divided by the contribution margin ratio
A lower break-even point means less risk—the business becomes profitable sooner

faq.question: How do you calculate the break-even point?
faq.answer: Break-even in units equals total fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit. For example, with $100,000 in fixed costs and a $20 contribution margin per unit, break-even is 5,000 units. In dollars, divide fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio.

faq.question: What does a high break-even point indicate about a business?
faq.answer: A high break-even point means the business needs to sell many units before becoming profitable, usually due to high fixed costs or low contribution margins. This increases risk because the business is more vulnerable to sales downturns below that threshold.
